articles.title: Indonesia: 13 dead in mine disaster that highlights illegal hunt for gold
articles.summary: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.
articles.body:
It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.

Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.

Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.

Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.

Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.

"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.

"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."

Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.

Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.

This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.

On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.

But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.

"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.

"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."

Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.

Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".

"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.

In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.

Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.

But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.

Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.

Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.

There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.

Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".

"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."

The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.

"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.

"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.

"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."

As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.

More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.

As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

articles.title: Australia’s Great Barrier Reef hosted the world’s first floating hotel in 1988; after a brief stay in Vietnam, the resort was relocated to North Korea
articles.summary: Explore the extraordinary journey of the world’s first floating hotel, once situated in Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, and its relocation challenges through Vietnam to North Korea, highlighting its impact on tourism and environmental assessments.
articles.body: In March 1988, visitors to Australia's Great Barrier Reef could book a stay at a hotel unlike any other. The seven-story Barrier Reef Floating Resort stood above John Brewer Reef, about 70 kilometres off the coast of Townsville, Queensland. Guests could enjoy views of the ocean from their rooms while having access to restaurants, bars, a nightclub, a swimming pool and a tennis court. The resort was known as the first floating hotel in the world. However, the period that this resort remained operational in Australia was no more than a year. Due to its financial problems, the building was relocated to Vietnam and then to North Korea. The hotel was developed by Doug Tarca, a Townsville developer. He had an intention to offer tourists an opportunity to have contact with the reef without having to return to the mainland. The company that undertook the construction of this hotel was Barrier Reef Holdings Limited.The floating hotel was built in SingaporeAccording to ABC News, the corporation engaged a company from Singapore for the construction of the hotel in 1986. Following the construction process, the building was then shipped to Australia on a heavy-lift ship and the MOUA Interpretation Manual puts that journey at over 5,000 kilometres. The building arrived at John Brewer Reef during the summer period of 1987 to 1988. The hotel contained 140 double rooms and 34 luxury suites, according to the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority. It had restaurants, bars, a nightclub, a helipad and a tennis court. Visitors could enjoy dining and snorkelling around the reef. Location was a reason that made this trip different, but at the same time there were certain inconveniences. The guests had to travel from Townsville by sea or helicopter and the weather could cause problems with communication between the hotel and the mainland. Weather conditions were affecting its functioning and the number of guests was declining gradually.The hotel moved to Vietnam after financial problemsThe resort was not attracting enough tourists to make it profitable in terms of covering its operating expenses. Due to being far away, harsh weather conditions and expensive running costs, the enterprise could not be run effectively. The owners were forced to sell the resort. About a year later, the hotel was sold to a company in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. It was taken 5,000 kilometres away from Australia and transported to Vietnam, where it docked in 1989. It was renamed Saigon Floating Hotel and moored on the Saigon River close to the Tran Hung Dao Statue. The floating hotel attracted tourists when it docked in Vietnam because this country was now trying to develop itself after the war. The locals referred to it as “The Floater”. It was a hotel with two nightclubs. The floating hotel operated from 1989 to 1997 in Vietnam, according to an ABC News story about its journey.Its next destination was North KoreaThe hotel was subsequently purchased by a South Korean firm and relocated to the Mount Kumgang tourist area of North Korea in 1998. It was rebranded as Hotel Haegumgang and became a part of a tourism project that aimed at attracting tourists to the location. The relocation occurred at a time when North and South Korea sought to normalise relations with each other. South Korean firms helped build the Mount Kumgang Resort, which became an important site for tourists from South Korea. The hotel was supposed to bring tourists to the North Korean resort and it did host South Korean visitors until tours to Mount Kumgang were halted in 2008. Tourism at Mount Kumgang was halted in July 2008 after a North Korean soldier shot and killed a 53-year-old South Korean tourist who had allegedly entered a restricted military zone.After the tours stopped, the hotel sat closed and dilapidated. According to Reuters, in October 2019, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un toured Mount Kumgang and criticised the state of tourist facilities there. According to him, these facilities were outdated and badly maintained and their demolition was needed. Among those facilities whose fate was uncertain was the Australian resort, according to ABC News. The report confirmed that the hotel was still in North Korea at the time. South Korean intelligence reports cited by CNN say the hotel was among the sites North Korea destroyed in 2022.A lasting legacy in AustraliaAccording to the MOUA Interpretation Manual, the floating hotel has covered more than 14,000 kilometres in about thirty years, having moved from Singapore to Australia's Great Barrier Reef, then to Vietnam and finally to North Korea. It became a unique part of world history because of its travel experience. Despite its short stay in Queensland, the project also had a lasting impact on how tourism developments were assessed in Great Barrier Reef Marine Park. According to the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority, the hotel project led to one of Australia's most complex environmental assessments at the time. The surveillance program also helped lay the standards for future developments within the marine park. The life of the resort was very short, but its travel through three nations made it noteworthy. This was a project that started out as a very big idea of building a luxurious resort above one of the world's most famous natural wonders, but it ended up as a floating hotel in North Korea.You use AI every day. articles.title: An 800-year-old Spanish monastery was dismantled, packed into 11,000 crates and shipped to America; decades later, its stones were rebuilt in Florida
articles.summary: Discover the incredible story of an 800-year-old Spanish monastery that was dismantled, shipped to America, and rebuilt in Florida. Learn about its historical significance and cultural impact.
articles.body: A 12th-century Spanish monastery made an unusual journey across the Atlantic in the 1920s. According to The Cultural Landscape Foundation, workers dismantled its stone cloisters and several other structures, packed them into approximately 11,000 wooden crates and shipped them to the United States. The plan was to rebuild the medieval complex in California. Instead, the stones lay in storage in New York for 26 years until they were moved to their current location in Florida. Nowadays, this rebuilt complex is called the Ancient Spanish Monastery. It can be found in North Miami Beach, far away from its original site in Spain.A monastery built in medieval SpainAccording to SAH Archipedia, the foundation date of the monastery is 1133 A.D. and it was located in Sacramenia, which is close to Segovia, northern Spain. Its construction was completed in 1141. According to SAH Archipedia, the monastery was originally built as the Cistercian Monastery of Our Lady, Queen of the Angels. It was renamed in honour of Bernard of Clairvaux when he was canonized in 1174. Cistercian monks inhabited the monastery for many years. The simplicity principle of these religious orders was illustrated in the Romanesque and Gothic style of the monastery. The relationship between the owners of the property and the community had altered during the ecclesiastical confiscations that occurred in the 1830s. According to the historical record of the monastery, the cloisters had been confiscated and sold afterward, and the premises were used as a granary and a stable.William Randolph Hearst bought the monasteryIn 1925, American newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst bought the monastery's cloisters as well as some additional buildings, according to the Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau. He intended to move them to his Californian mansion of San Simeon and reconstruct them in that location. The buildings were taken apart stone by stone. They were numbered to ease their identification in the future, then wrapped in hay and put into roughly 11,000 wooden boxes and about 33,000 stone blocks were in the shipment. The boxes landed in New York, but an outbreak of hoof and mouth disease in Spain led to difficulties. According to Florida International University's student news site, the U.S. Department of Agriculture had the crates dismantled and the hay burned to avoid spreading the disease. Once the hay was burned, the stones were put back into the boxes in the wrong order, which scrambled the number sequence and complicated the stones' identification. Another factor that prevented Hearst from fulfilling his project was the Great Depression.The stones found a new home in FloridaFollowing the death of Hearst in 1951, Florida businessman Raymond Moss and William Edgemon bought the dismantled remains in 1952. They intended to reconstruct the building as an attraction in South Florida. The containers were shipped to Miami, where the stonemason Allan Carswell oversaw the reconstruction process. It involved the fitting of several thousand stones without depending on the numbering system.The project took 19 months and cost 1.5 million dollars at the time, according to the Society of Architectural Historians. The rebuilt complex included the original cloisters, chapter house, and refectory. The original church and other monastery structures remained in Spain. The Florida site was therefore for a reconstruction using medieval components rather than an entire monastery moved intact across the ocean.A medieval landmark in modern FloridaBishop Henry Louttit bought the monastery in 1964 for the Episcopal Diocese of South Florida. Financial difficulties later forced the Diocese of South Florida to sell the complex to Colonel Robert Pentland Jr., who donated it to the newly formed Episcopal Diocese of Southeast Florida. It became the Parish of Saint Bernard de Clairvaux and continues to be a functioning house of worship, with grounds dating back to the 1950s that recreate Spanish monastic gardens with paved paths, fountains and neatly kept plantings. This place was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972. Visitors can stroll along its cloisters and gardens situated in North Miami Beach today. The history of the monastery includes several decades of uncertainty, a messed-up numbering and a long period of reconstruction. Presently, the medieval stones serve as part of a functioning church in Florida, thousands of miles away from the Spanish settlement where the buildings originally belonged.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK signs £8bn deal to ensure submarines are 'warfighting ready'
articles.summary: The deal will allow "work around the clock to get our submarines back out to sea" , Wes Streeting says.
articles.body:
The UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

The five-year deal, awarded to defence firm Babcock, will create 3,000 new jobs and around 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles mainly across Plymouth, Clyde and Bristol, the MoD said.

It will allow the Royal Navy to "work around the clock to get our submarines back out to sea" and see naval base services modernised, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it demonstrated his commitment to "keeping the public safe" and "providing opportunities to "get young people into work".

"We're providing opportunities to get young people into work, to bring jobs to communities in Plymouth, Clyde and beyond, and to boost growth across the UK," the prime minister added.

Streeting said: "We're not going to repeat the mistakes of the past, where investment in our nuclear capability was delayed.

"Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain warfighting ready."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast during a visit to HMNB Devonport on Thursday, the defence secretary described the investment as a "win for the Navy… for jobs and the taxpayer."

He said the structure of the contract incentivises Babcock to produce results, adding "the more productive they are, the more they earn but if they fall short, then they don't get paid as much".

Streeting was also asked about reports that 100,000 military reservists who previously served in the armed forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

"What we're doing today is contacting our strategic reserves to make sure their contact details are up to date and we have those details to hand and this is all part of our readiness picture," he said.

The funding is part of a wider £26bn investment into the UK's naval bases announced earlier this year.

First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said it will allow the Navy to "tackle delays that hold us back" by "getting submarines through maintenance quicker and back where they belong: beneath the waves".

Harry Holt, Babcock's chief executive, said: "We are very proud at Babcock of the critical support that we provide to the Royal Navy, in particular our unwavering support to the continuous at sea deterrent – the UK's highest defence priority."

articles.title: BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend 2027 heads to Brighton
articles.summary: The annual music festival will take place in Preston Park from Friday 28 to Sunday 30 May next year.
articles.body:
BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend is heading to Brighton for 2027, it has been announced.

The annual music festival will take place in Preston Park from Friday 28 to Sunday 30 May next year.

Radio 1 Breakfast Show host Greg James told listeners he is "so excited" to bring the festival to the city as he revealed the news on air, adding: "It's going to be amazing".

Tens of thousands of fans are expected to attend the three-day event, which will feature about 70 acts, from some of the biggest names in music to new emerging artists.

Big Weekend, BBC Radio 1's flagship event, is held in a new location each year - often in towns and cities that don't get as many big live music events.

In previous years acts such as US pop star Taylor Swift came to Norwich and Swansea, grime star Stormzy performed in Exeter, pop rock band The 1975 headlined in Dundee and US singer Bruno Mars featured in Londonderry.

Breakfast host Greg said: "If Radio 1 was a place, it would be Brighton.

"It's got an amazing musical heritage, loves bringing different people together and wants to make sure fun is prioritised.

"It's actually stupid that it's taken so long for us to do a Big Weekend there. Sorry about that."

Earlier this year the event was held in Sunderland's Herrington Country Park, where about 100,000 music fans basked in the the sun while dancing to a host of major artists.

Grammy and Brit Awards winner Olivia Dean, Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and veteran DJ Fatboy Slim topped the bill across the weekend.

Irish star CMAT, Messy singer Lola Young, former One Directioner Niall Horan and American singer Kehlani were also on the line-up.

The vibrancy of the current electronic music scene led Radio 1 to dedicate day one of Big Weekend to its Dance Party brand for the first time.

It spanned styles, backgrounds and generations - with local lad Max Jones getting the party started on the Introducing stage, and Fisher, MK and Clementine Douglas keeping the party going throughout the day.

Big Weekend tickets are usually significantly cheaper than most major festivals, with a proportion reserved for local residents.

It has not yet been revealed when tickets will go on sale for the 2027 event and at what price.

Details about the line-up will be announced in the coming months, BBC Radio 1 said.

articles.title: How fake gangster identities are keeping Bollywood and Mumbai police on edge
articles.summary: MUMBAI: From luxury homes and expensive cars to red-carpet appearances and millions of followers, celebrity life often looks enviable from the outside.
articles.body: MUMBAI: From luxury homes and expensive cars to red-carpet appearances and millions of followers, celebrity life often looks enviable from the outside. But being famous also means living with a level of visibility most people never experience.Their homes are known, their movements are followed, and even a routine outing can attract attention. For some, that visibility can become a source of fear.That fear takes on a different dimension when a threatening message arrives, demanding crores of rupees or invoking the name of a notorious gangster.The sender may claim to belong to an organised crime network, know details about a celebrity's life or threaten those close to them. But is the person really connected to the gang whose name they are using?Recent investigations into threats against Bollywood personalities have exposed a worrying possibility for police: criminals may be borrowing the identities and reputations of notorious gangsters to make their threats appear credible, even when they have no established links to those gangs.The names are familiar. The people using them, however, may not be.The distinction became clear in the case of actor Tusshar Kapoor. His team received an audio message from a person claiming to be Harry Boxer, an alleged member of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. The caller demanded Rs 5 crore.The threat prompted Kapoor to alert Mumbai Police, following which the police protection branch enhanced security for him and his sister, producer Ekta Kapoor. But the investigation took an unexpected turn. The Crime Branch's technical team compared the voice in the recording with available official samples of Boxer and found no match, according to police sources.Days later, police arrested Vaibhav Chandra Mishra, 30, an unemployed IIT graduate from Bengaluru, for allegedly sending threatening audio messages to actor Ayushmann Khurrana through Instagram.Police said he had no links to any gang. Officials later informed that Mishra had allegedly used artificial intelligence to issue the threats.The two cases have no confirmed connection. But they raise the same question for investigators: is a notorious gang actually behind a threat, or is someone simply using its name to create fear?A borrowed identityIn the Tusshar Kapoor case, police suspect an unidentified person impersonated a gang member or used artificial intelligence tools to create a voice resembling Boxer's. Senior officials said the threat appeared to be an attempt to exploit the fear surrounding the Bishnoi gang and extort money from Bollywood personalities.No FIR had been registered when the initial reports were published. The probe was handed to the Crime Branch's Anti-Extortion Cell.In Mishra's case, investigators traced him to Bengaluru through technical analysis of the Instagram accounts allegedly used to send the messages."Prima facie, he has admitted to sending threats to Khurrana through Instagram," DCP (crime) Raj Tilak Roshan said."However, we suspect that he had created multiple fictitious Instagram accounts and may have sent threatening messages to a few other celebrities as well. This is being verified," he added.Police said preliminary investigations suggested Mishra had sent the messages out of frustration. An official informed that he had no gang links. It remains unclear whether he had any role in the threat received by Kapoor.The use of a gang's identity is not limited to threatening audio messages. In an alleged extortion plot involving actor Salman Khan, police uncovered what they described as a fabricated trail of WhatsApp chats and identities designed to make it appear that an organised crime gang was threatening him.Investigators found inconsistencies in the chats, while CCTV footage did not support the accused's claims. He allegedly admitted to fabricating the story to extort money. Police were also examining whether he had acted alone.The latest case involving Saif Ali Khan has presented investigators with another verification challenge.The actor reportedly received a death threat from a person claiming to be Zeeshan Akhtar, a wanted accused in the Baba Siddique murder case. Police are checking whether Akhtar actually issued the threat or whether someone was impersonating him.When a name carries its own threatThe reputation attached to these gang names is not without context. The October 18 firing incident targeting actor Tiger Shroff in Juhu, in which the Crime Branch arrested several accused, heightened security concerns among Bollywood personalities. Police have alleged that the attack was part of a larger organised crime conspiracy.But a genuine attack and an impersonated threat are not the same thing. The fear generated by one can make the other more convincing.Harry Boxer, whose name surfaced in the threat to Kapoor, has also been linked in police reports to firing incidents, including the attack on comedian Kapil Sharma's cafe in Canada last year. Invoking a name associated with such incidents can give an otherwise unidentified caller an immediate air of credibility.A separate investigation into threats received by actor Ranveer Singh and filmmaker Rohit Shetty also shows why police are cautious about accepting claims of responsibility at face value.The two received a threatening audio clip from a person identifying himself as Boxer. The speaker accused Singh of going back on his word, threatened his staff and their families, and warned Shetty and the wider film industry to fall in line.However, Crime Branch officials said the clip's authenticity had not been established. Police were examining whether the voice belonged to a genuine gang member or had been generated using artificial intelligence.Officers also said they had no records of the individuals claiming responsibility and sought technical assistance from police forces across the country. Singh and Shetty told police they had never communicated with the Bishnoi gang.How police verify a threatFor investigators, establishing who is behind a threat involves more than identifying the name or gang invoked in a message.In Kapoor's case, the Crime Branch compared the threatening audio with available voice samples of Boxer. In Khurrana's case, technical analysis of Instagram accounts helped investigators trace the accused to Bengaluru.The Salman Khan investigation involved a different set of checks. Police examined the alleged WhatsApp conversations, compared the claims with CCTV footage and recovered two mobile phones that the accused had allegedly hidden near the Bandra seafront. Screenshots of the chats were also seized in the presence of witnesses.In the Ranveer Singh-Shetty case, police sought technical assistance to establish the authenticity of the audio clip and verify the identity of the person claiming responsibility.Each investigation has followed a different trail. But the common challenge is to separate the identity claimed by the sender from the person actually behind the message.Shreya Joshi, a resident of Dadar, expressed her genuine fear of threats and extortion even for commoners. “Honestly, it is frightening because you can’t tell whether a threat is genuine or someone is bluffing. When someone uses a gangster’s identity, you naturally worry about your safety and your family. With AI, even voice messages can be misleading. The uncertainty is what makes the entire situation especially scary.”The cost of doubtFor the police, such threats create a difficult balance. An unverified message cannot automatically be treated as an organised gang operation. But it cannot be dismissed simply because the sender's identity is doubtful.Kapoor's security was enhanced even as investigators questioned whether the caller was genuinely linked to Boxer. In Saif Ali Khan's case, police are still verifying the identity of the person who allegedly issued the threat. The Ranveer Singh-Shetty audio, too, remains under examination.There is also a larger concern for officials. When the same gang name appears in threats from different people, it can create the impression of a single organised network at work, even when the cases may have no connection.Speaking to TOI, Hemangini Jain, a Delhi high court advocate, said, "Ordinary citizens are equally vulnerable, if not more, because unlike celebrities, they may not have the resources or access to seek immediate security. Anyone can misuse a gangster's name to intimidate or extort money, and the victim may have no way of knowing whether the threat is genuine."This creates a serious sense of insecurity, particularly when one's family and personal safety are involved. The concern is that fear itself becomes a tool of extortion, regardless of whether the threatener has any actual criminal connections," adv Jain added.The investigations do not establish that every threat invoking a gangster's name is fake, or that organised crime networks are not behind some of them. They do, however, underline why police are looking beyond the name in a threatening message and trying to establish who is actually responsible.For the person receiving it, the name may be enough to trigger fear. For police officials, it is only the beginning of the probe.The name is not proof, and the threat alone does not establish a gang connection. articles.title: Mark Rothko painting bought for $115,000 in 1983 sells for $17.7 million at Sotheby's New York auction, giving collectors Theodore and Ruth Baum a return of more than 150 times
articles.summary: Mark Rothko's Untitled from 1967 has sold for $17.7 million at Sotheby's in New York, more than 150 times the $115,000 that collectors Theodore and Ruth
articles.body: Mark Rothko's Untitled from 1967 has sold for $17.7 million at Sotheby's in New York, more than 150 times the $115,000 that collectors Theodore and Ruth Baum paid for the painting in 1983. The couple held the work for 43 years before it went under the hammer on 16 November, where it finished above the top of its pre-sale estimate range. Rothko painted it in the final years of his life, using fiery red and brilliant tangerine, and the Baums acquired it as their first contemporary artwork. That purchase began more than two decades of passionate collecting for the couple.From a $115,000 purchase to a $17.7 million sale: How Theodore and Baum’s ‘Vision’ performed at the New York auctionAccording to Luxury.it, the Rothko was offered on Monday 16 November in ‘Vision: The Extraordinary Collection of Theodore and Ruth Baum,’ a 6 pm evening auction. The sale formed part of The New York Sales, held at the Breuer Building from 16 to 19 November. The painting carried a pre-sale estimate of $10 million to $15 million.Why red mattered: Rothko's 1967 canvas and the colour thread through the Baum collectionSotheby's says red is perhaps Rothko's most important colour, both symbolically and aesthetically, and that this canvas shows his command of colour in conveying the breadth of human emotion. The same colour runs through the Baum collection, from Ellsworth Kelly's Red White to Lucio Fontana's slashed red canvas Concetto spaziale, Attese, and Ed Ruscha's Dimple.Baum collection results at Sotheby's: Joan Mitchell leads while all 24 works find buyersThe collection made $109.9 million with fees, and every one of its 24 lots sold. Joan Mitchell's Green Book of Barbara Guest was the top lot at $19.3 million, against the $65,000 the couple paid in 1986. Andy Warhol's The Scream (After Munch), from 1984, made $7.9 million. A third of the lots sold below their low estimates and a quarter above their high ones.Sotheby's New York evening totals $378.7 million as Yayoi Kusama sets a $15 million recordThe Baum sale was one of two evening auctions that night. Together with The Now and Contemporary Evening, which made $268.7 million, it brought in $378.7 million with fees. Luxury.it reports that Yayoi Kusama's No. 3P.B., a 1960 Infinity Nets painting, sold for $15 million, a new auction record for the artist, who died in August at 97. Roy Lichtenstein's Reflections on "Painter and Model" led the night at $24.6 million.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Congo Ebola outbreak crosses 12,000 cases as fighting disrupts response
articles.summary: Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) has crossed 12,000 confirmed cases, according to government data released on Thursday.
articles.body: Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) has crossed 12,000 confirmed cases, according to government data released on Thursday.Clashes between rebel groups and the army are disrupting efforts to control the spread of the disease, reported by news agency AP.The outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic in history, with 12,021 confirmed cases and nearly half of those infected having died, data from Congo's Health Ministry showed.It is also the deadliest among the country's 17 Ebola outbreaks and could surpass the West African epidemic of 2014-2016, which claimed around 11,000 lives.Declared in May, the current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccine or treatment is available. Health teams are struggling to contain the disease amid armed conflict, poor road connectivity and resistance from residents driven by mistrust and misinformation.Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of infected people, including those who have died from the disease. Containment efforts require the early identification and isolation of patients, monitoring of people who may have been exposed and safe burial of victims.Fighting between the Congolese army and the convention pour la revolution populaire (CRP) rebels resumed on Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 km north of Bunia.The clashes forced more people to flee towards Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a key centre for the Ebola response.The CRP is among more than 100 armed groups operating in eastern Congo, where prolonged conflict has fuelled a severe humanitarian crisis. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International criminal court in 2012 for recruiting and using children under 15 in armed conflict.Earlier clashes between the army and rebels had prevented health teams from reaching some communities, disrupted the monitoring of people exposed to the virus and reduced staffing at some treatment centres, said Dr Catherine Smallwood, the world health organization's Ebola incident manager, on Wednesday.She further said, around a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday. They had been trapped for three days in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Britain net migration falls to 77,000, lowest level since 1997 outside pandemic
articles.summary: Recent data reveals that Britain's net migration has fallen to 77,000, the lowest level since 1997, raising concerns about the economy and political landscape surrounding immigration.
articles.body: Britain's annual net migration fell to 77,000 in the year to June, marking its lowest level in nearly three decades outside the COVID-19 pandemic, according to official figures released on Thursday. The decline offers some relief to the Labour government amid continued political pressure over immigration, but economists have warned that a shrinking migrant workforce could weigh on economic growth.Data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed that net migration dropped from 204,000 in the 12 months to June last year to 77,000 in the latest reporting period.The latest figure takes net migration down by around 90% from its peak in 2023, when the number of people arriving in Britain exceeded those leaving by nearly one million.The decline also brings migration closer to levels that successive governments have sought to achieve. Former Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron pledged in 2010 to bring annual net migration down to the "tens of thousands", although his government did not meet that target.Despite the sharp fall, immigration continues to feature prominently in Britain's political debate. A YouGov poll published this week found that it was the second-biggest concern among voters, behind the economy, Reuters reported.The issue has remained politically contentious for more than a decade, with both legal migration and unauthorised arrivals shaping public debate. Concerns about immigration from the European Union were among the factors that influenced the 2016 Brexit referendum.The latest reduction in net migration follows restrictions introduced by previous governments on work visas. These included limits on migrants bringing family dependents to Britain and higher salary requirements intended to prioritise skilled workers with graduate-level qualifications.The Labour government has indicated that it plans to impose further restrictions. Earlier this month, it announced proposals to double the standard qualifying period for permanent settlement from five years to 10 years, as public concern over immigration continued.Migration has played a significant role in changing Britain's population over the past 30 years. Arrivals increased following the European Union's 2004 expansion and rose again after Brexit in 2020. Net migration subsequently reached a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023, before beginning its steep decline.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi on Thursday took a swipe at Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, saying neither would become the chief minister after the 2027 assembly elections.Addressing the Samajik Parivartan Morcha's first joint rally in Lucknow, he said the next chief minister would be someone with a moustache, in an apparent reference to alliance partner Chandrashekhar Azad."Someone remarked that this is an alliance between the bearded and the moustachioed. And, in truth, it is. Now, I wish to address that clean-shaven face and the other clean-shaved head, you will not become the CM anymore; it will be someone with a moustache..," he said.Owaisi accused the BJP and the Samajwadi Party of failing to protect the Constitution and ensure adequate political representation for Muslims.Invoking Dr BR Ambedkar, he said the Constitution guaranteed liberty, fraternity, justice and equality. He accused the RSS and the Sangh Parivar of working against these principles."Justice will not come through bulldozers or encounters. Justice will come through Babasaheb Ambedkar's Constitution. The rule of law will be restored," he said, targeting the BJP government.He also criticised the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging that it was being used to weaken the Constitution.Targeting the Samajwadi Party, Owaisi accused its leadership of practising caste-based politics and seeking Muslim votes without ensuring adequate representation to the community."How many times will we be betrayed? Akhilesh Yadav, will you give a ticket to a Muslim from Karhal?" he asked. Yadav had won the Karhal seat in the 2022 Assembly elections.Owaisi accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Adityanath of promoting communal divisions while failing to address unemployment and concerns over education.He said the Morcha, if voted to power, would focus on education and employment for young people."We will ensure education for young people and jobs after they complete their education. We will make doctors and engineers, and ensure that our students get opportunity to study in IITs," he said.Referring to the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, Owaisi urged people to support the Morcha's candidates in the 2027 elections."The historic opportunity before us is that we should support neither the red cap (of Samajwadi Party) nor the RSS-BJP," he said.Praising Azad, Owaisi said he could represent the poor, oppressed and deprived sections of society."If there can be a chief minister in Uttar Pradesh who represents the poor, the oppressed and the deprived, and whose government will be of the people rather than only a particular section, his name will be Chandrashekhar Azad," he said."I am confident that with our unity, prayers and hard work, we will make Chandrashekhar Azad the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh. articles.title: Trump's DC renovation fund gets mystery $300 million donation: Report
articles.summary: A startling $300 million donation to a National Park Service fund supporting President Trump's renovation projects has emerged, with the donor's identity shrouded in mystery, prompting questions about potential government favoritism.
articles.body: A National Park Service fund used to finance projects backed by US President Donald Trump received a mysterious $300 million contribution in September, but the donor’s identity remains secret, according to a report by The New York Times.The payment was made to a National Park Service bank account that has been used to support several renovation initiatives favoured by Trump, including the proposed White House ballroom and refurbishment of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Neither the administration nor existing records have identified the source of the latest contribution.The fund was initially created to collect charitable donations for national parks and historically received less than $100 million a year. However, its collections have risen sharply since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, reaching approximately $790 million, NYT reported.The unusually large September deposit came to light after Tony Irish, a veteran attorney at the Department of the Interior, examined the account's contributions. The department had expected donations of around $50 million for the month but received approximately $347 million instead.The discrepancy raised questions about the source of the money and whether contributors could be seeking favourable treatment from the government."Are the donors seeking certain government benefits?" Irish told NYT. "We just don't know, because of the lack of transparency."A separate report by The Washington Post identified several major corporate contributors to Trump's capital renovation projects. These include technology companies Apple, NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft, as well as defence contractor Lockheed Martin.The National Park Service account is separate from the Trust for the National Mall, a non-profit organisation collecting pledges specifically for the White House ballroom project.The White House and the Department of the Interior declined to provide details about the individual donors. Instead, the administration defended Trump's efforts to renovate and improve the US capital."President Donald J. Trump has done more to make our nation's capital a shining beacon than any other president in the history of this country," a spokesperson said.The spokesperson added that previous administrations had allowed Washington, DC, to deteriorate, while Trump had made the city "safe and beautiful again". The statement also described the president as an "expert builder" and praised his involvement in the city's transformation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: UK reservists contacted as 'threat environment' rises, Streeting says
articles.summary: It comes after reports that reservists have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

It comes after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," Streeting told Today.

"We saw last Friday a very serious incident – the incursion into Polish airspace by Russian missiles, we've seen state-sponsored terrorism waged by Russia across Europe, we've obviously had incidents concerning Iran around RAF bases here in the UK.

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks."

He added: "Because the more ready we are the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war, that is my goal, that is the goal of this government."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast that "if, God forbid, this country did find itself at war" and there was then an inquiry, the Ministry of Defence would be criticised if the government had not kept its records up-to-date."

This is not a case of pressing the panic button for imminent war, but more one of good housekeeping.

When Britain went to war in Iraq in 2003 the MoD had a poor grasp of who might be available to serve, what current skills they had and what their up-to-date contact details were. So they obviously don't want to be in that situation if there is a national crisis in the future that triggers a mobilisation.

Twenty three years on, the Ukraine war has changed everything. It's brought a hot war to the very borders of Nato, it's exposed the dangers of having too few troops available, but most of all it has changed the nature of warfare.

People who have spent their adult lives never touching a weapon can turn out to be extraordinarily skilled drone operators, those with a talent for electronics, radio and signals work have a vital role to play in electronic warfare.

So this exercise by the government, probably long overdue, is about knowing who can do what and where they can be contacted.

Justin Crump, a former Army officer and now CEO of the business intelligence firm Sibylline, told the BBC: "Ukraine has shown us the importance of mobilising civilian skills and approaches in modern warfare. This is a first step, and an overdue one in many ways, with the effort likely to increase through early 2027. [It is] very much a part of deterrence and not an intention to use people".

He said veterans - a sometimes misleading term for men and women who are often in peak physical shape and fitness - that he has contacted have generally responded positively to the move. "After all", he said, "they signed up to help before, but want to make sure their enhanced skills and talents are valued".

The MoD's decision to contact ex-military personnel comes after news that the UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which the defence secretary said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

Meanwhile, Streeting also praised the Duke of Sussex's "patriotic spirit" after the former soldier said he would rejoin the armed forces again if needed.

Asked whether there could be a role for Harry, the defence secretary told Today: "I'm always happy to talk to him about how we can work together, whether that's through his Invictus Games, which does a brilliant job supporting our veterans and giving them opportunities to take part in those amazing and inspiring competitive sporting events, but he does have experience to bring to bear."

Streeting praised the "service he's given to our country" and the fact he had spoken about his "willingness and readiness to serve".

"I think that's exactly the sort of patriotic spirit we're looking for," he said.

"I think it's that sort of patriotic spirit we'll find throughout our strategic reserve."

Last week, Harry, who spent a decade in the forces and served on the front line in Afghanistan, said: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

articles.title: US Army calls Iowa blast of nearly 5 tonnes of toxic explosives a ‘huge success’ after health fears
articles.summary: The US military has described the controlled detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa as a “huge success”, after the operation sparked
articles.body: The US military has described the controlled detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa as a “huge success”, after the operation sparked widespread concerns over potential health and environmental risks among residents.Smoke was seen rising shortly after 9 am local time (2 pm GMT) on Wednesday as the US Army detonated the volatile explosives at an ammunition plant near Middletown. Officials later said the risk from the operation had been reduced to “as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible”.The blast followed weeks of uncertainty, public protests and legal challenges, with the Army repeatedly postponing the operation over concerns about possible lead contamination.In an update on Wednesday evening, the Army said the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) had issued an “all clear” around the ammunition plant. It also reported no airborne lead detection following the explosion.US President Donald Trump welcomed the outcome, saying mitigation efforts had exceeded expectations.“The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success,” acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle wrote on social media.Officials report no airborne lead after explosionThe explosives, which had been stored for around 20 years, contained lead azide, a highly volatile compound that had deteriorated through a process known as recrystallisation. This made the material increasingly vulnerable to accidental detonation through friction or movement.The US Army had warned residents about the possibility of exposure to toxic lead dust before the operation. Lead exposure poses serious health risks, particularly for children and pregnant women, and no level of exposure is considered safe.Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin said that all agency air monitors continued to report zero detection of airborne lead in the hours following the blast.The Army said post-detonation surface sampling was underway and that the results would be made public once testing was complete.FEMA administrator Cameron Hamilton said additional resources and testing would be provided in the coming days and weeks.Residents relieved but calls for more testingThe explosion brought relief to several residents who had spent days preparing for the operation.Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC that he was relieved after watching the blast from his workplace, around eight miles from the site. He also monitored a camera at his home, located about a mile from the ammunition plant.“We did not feel anything. We did not see anything,” he said.Resident Sandy Mabeus, who lives around eight miles away, said her family had shut the windows and garage, brought their outdoor cat inside and watched the explosion through three separate livestreams.“We did not feel or hear a thing here,” she told the BBC, adding that she had to check the videos to make sure the explosion had actually taken place.Iowa farmer David Vandenberg, who lives about 20 miles from the site, said he heard a rumble around 9 am but neither saw nor smelled anything. Officials had collected samples from his yard and pond ahead of the detonation.He said he expected further testing but was pleased that the explosion appeared to have remained contained.Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also said his state was seeing little to no impact from the blast. Illinois shares a border with Iowa, with the detonation site located around 10 miles away.However, concerns over the operation have not entirely subsided. Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand called for further testing and transparency, criticising the chaotic preparations ahead of the explosion.He said residents affected by the operation must receive immediate assistance.Legal challenges delayed Army operationThe Army had faced significant opposition from residents and politicians over its plans to destroy the ageing explosives.The detonation was scheduled and postponed several times in recent weeks as officials prepared for colder winter temperatures and assessed the risks.Authorities had introduced an optional evacuation zone and advised residents to shelter in place ahead of the explosion.Legal challenges were also filed seeking to stop the operation on environmental and public health grounds. However, an appeals court on Monday overturned an earlier decision that had halted the detonation.While acknowledging the concerns raised by residents, the court concluded that the danger posed by an accidental explosion was greater than the risks associated with the controlled blast.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Rahul must apologise': Nitin Nabin targets Congress over Ambedkar at Patna event
articles.summary: BJP national president Nitin Nabin on Thursday demanded an apology from Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over the insults allegedly heaped on Dr BR Ambedkar
articles.body: BJP national president Nitin Nabin on Thursday demanded an apology from Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over the insults allegedly heaped on Dr BR Ambedkar by the Congress. He accused the party of failing to uphold the constitutional values laid down by the architect of the Constitution.Addressing the BJP's Samvidhan Gaurav Diwas event in Patna, Nabin accused the Congress of repeatedly undermining the Constitution for its political interests. He also questioned the party's record of dismissing elected state governments during its rule at the Centre, PTI reported."Congress dismissed 90 state governments while it was in power at the Centre," Nabin said, adding that former prime minister Indira Gandhi alone had dismissed more than 50 state governments during her tenure.Nabin further alleged that the Congress had failed to follow the principles laid down by Ambedkar in the Constitution, while praising Prime Minister Narendra Modi for upholding them."Congress did not live up to the standards laid down in the Constitution drafted by Ambedkar, but Narendra Modi did," he said.Invoking India's cultural and spiritual heritage, Nabin said the framers of the Constitution drew inspiration from the reign of Lord Ram."I feel that the framers of the Constitution drew immense inspiration from the reign of Lord Shri Ram," he said.He also referred to the depictions of Lord Buddha and Lord Mahavira in the Constitution, highlighting Bihar's association with both figures."When Lord Buddha and Lord Mahavira are depicted in Parts V and VI of the Constitution, the karmabhoomi of both is our own Bihar," Nabin said."The soul of this Constitution and its provisions were framed by carrying forward our culture and our heritage," he added.Nabin also invoked Vande Mataram, recalling former president Dr Rajendra Prasad's recognition of the song as a symbol of the freedom struggle on January 24, 1950. He said the complete version of the song was sung at the Red Fort on August 15, 2026, adding that it made Indians proud of the Constitution's original spirit.He further accused the Congress of sacrificing the Constitution for its vested interests.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Youth's body found hanging from tree in Buxar village
articles.summary: Buxar: Missing 25-year-old Golu Kumar Singh found hanging from a tree near Shahipur village; police probe underway, postmortem awaited amid foul play claims.
articles.body: Buxar: The body of a 25-year-old man, who had been missing for two days, was found hanging from a tree in an agricultural field near Shahipur village under Itadhi police station area in Buxar on Thursday. The deceased was identified as Golu Kumar Singh, son of Baban Singh Koiry, a resident of the village.According to family members, Golu had been missing from home for the past two days. His family was searching for him when villagers spotted his body hanging from a tree in an orchard south of the village and informed police. Itadhi police reached the spot, took custody of the body and launched an investigation. A forensic science laboratory (FSL) team also visited the spot and collected evidence.Family members alleged that Golu had a dispute with some youths from a neighbouring village before his disappearance. Suspecting foul play, they alleged that he was killed and his body was later hanged from the tree to make the death appear to be a suicide. Golu is survived by a son.Itadhi SHO Pooja Kumari said the body was being sent for postmortem. “The exact cause of death will be known after the postmortem report. Police are investigating the matter based on the information provided by the family. articles.title: 'Abdul won't lay carpets': Chandrashekhar Azad, Asaduddin Owaisi promise Muslim deputy CM in UP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Azad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) chief Chandrashekhar Azad on Thursday promised a Muslim deputy chief minister if the Samajik Parivartan Morcha
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Azad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) chief Chandrashekhar Azad on Thursday promised a Muslim deputy chief minister if the Samajik Parivartan Morcha forms the next government in Uttar Pradesh after the 2027 assembly elections. Addressing the alliance's rally in Lucknow on Constitution Day, Azad also said a leader from the backward communities would be appointed to the post."Bring our rule, and Abdul will sit alongside Chandrashekhar Azad as Deputy Chief Minister and become the strength of the underprivileged. Abdul will become Deputy Chief Minister; Abdul will not lay carpets for anyone anymore; he will sit alongside Chandrashekhar Azad," news agency ANI quoted Azad as saying."Power will be in his hands; he will resolve your grievances, and he will not lay floor mats for others. 'Asad bhai' (Asaduddin Owaisi) also wanted to know what Abdul will do. Alongside Abdul, we will also make a person from the most backward/backward communities a deputy chief minister, mark my words," he added.Azad is the Morcha's chief ministerial candidate. He and AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi announced their alliance on November 12. The combine plans to contest all 403 Assembly seats in the state.Owaisi targeted SP chief Akhilesh Yadav asking him if he would "give a ticket to a Muslim from Karhal?"“Those who have come after our beard, listen—you keep one too. Bhaiya will talk about nepotism while working for his own dynasty. Will Akhilesh give a ticket to a Muslim from Karhal? You are losing because you people practice casteism. From places where Muslim MPs and MLAs used to be elected, Akhilesh Yadav is appointing his own family members," he said."You will have to give an answer, Akhilesh Yadav: when shameless dancing took place in Saifai and dancers came from Mumbai for two hours at a time, at that very time people in Muzaffarnagar were suffering and dying from the cold. Akhilesh Yadav has adopted the ideology of Hindutva; if you want proof, watch what is going to happen on 12 December—he is going out carrying the message of Hindutva. Listen Akhilesh Yadav, you are just getting Muslim votes and making Abdul lay out the carpets. Now Abdul will not lay out the carpets; I am not going to be afraid," he added.Addressing Muslim voters, Azad urged them to stop supporting parties without seeking adequate political representation. He described the 2027 election as a fight for the community's political existence and self-respect in Uttar Pradesh."My brothers of the Muslim community, this is no ordinary battle. This is not a struggle to remain someone's tail—this is a matter of self-respect and pride...This battle is for your own political existence in Uttar Pradesh. Understand this and resolve that you will no longer follow behind anyone," he said.The decision to project Azad as its chief ministerial candidate places a prominent Dalit leader at the forefront of the alliance with Owaisi's AIMIM. The combine is seeking to bring Dalit and Muslim voters together on a common political platform ahead of the 2027 assembly elections.For AIMIM, the partnership offers an opportunity to expand its political presence in Uttar Pradesh, where it failed to win a seat in the 2022 assembly elections. articles.title: World Hindu Congress 2026 to draw 4,500 delegates from 60 countries in Mumbai
articles.summary: The fourth edition of the World Hindu Congress (WHC), a global gathering of Hindu leaders, thinkers and professionals, will be held in Mumbai next month,
articles.body: The fourth edition of the World Hindu Congress (WHC), a global gathering of Hindu leaders, thinkers and professionals, will be held in Mumbai next month, with more than 4,500 delegates from over 60 countries expected to attend, organisers said on Thursday.According to news agency PTI report, the three-day event will begin on December 18 at the jio world convention centre in Mumbai's Bandra-Kurla complex. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat will address the inaugural session, according to Swami Vigyananand, initiator of the WHC and joint general secretary of the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP).Speaking at a press conference at the Press Club Kolkata, Vigyananand said the congress would feature more than 45 sessions and over 150 speakers. Participants will include representatives from the fields of business, politics, education, media, technology, culture and social organisations.The theme of the 2026 congress is 'Samanam Vratam Saha Chittam – shared commitment, collective resolve'. The event aims to bring together the global Hindu community to discuss the future of Hindu society and its contribution to the world.The congress will feature four special plenary sessions – Dharma, Samaj, Vishwakarma and Bhasha. These sessions will focus on spiritual traditions, social cohesion, skills and entrepreneurship, and linguistic heritage.Vigyananand also announced the launch of the first-ever World Hindu Expo alongside the congress. The expo aims to promote trade and commerce and create opportunities for economic growth within the Hindu community.According to the organisers, Hindus form a global community of more than 1.2 billion people spread across nearly 180 countries.The World Hindu Congress is organised every four years. Its previous editions were held in New Delhi in 2014, Chicago in 2018 and Bangkok in 2023. Organisers said representatives from government, industry, technology, media and culture have confirmed their participation in the 2026 edition.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: COIMBATORE: Coimbatore district cybercrime police have registered a case against an unidentified person who cheated a woman of Rs 2.5 lakh on the pretext of offering her an online part-time job.The victim, S Josephine Mary, 25, of Kallapalayam near Sulur in the district, was searching for a part-time job online when she came into contact with an unidentified person through Instagram and WhatsApp. The fraudster introduced her to a Telegram link to ‘Flipkart-TTCC’ platform and promised high returns if she invested money through it. Believing their claims, she initially paid Rs 800.Between March 12 and 14, 2024, she transferred a total of Rs 2.5 lakh in several instalments from her bank account to various bank accounts provided by the fraudster. However, neither the promised returns nor her principal amount was returned. When the fraudster demanded an additional Rs 1 lakh, she realised that she had been cheated.Based on her complaint, the district cybercrime police registered a case under Section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 66(D) of the Information Technology Act. articles.title: Is Poundland's US owner to blame for its collapse?
articles.summary: Poundland's management and MPs blame the retailer's owners, Gordon Brothers, but the US firm says without them the chain would have collapsed last year.
articles.body:
The blame game for the demise of Poundland is in full swing.

The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already.

Gordon Brothers stand to get paid back a further £22.5m, as their share of an existing £30m loan is set to be one of the first debts that the administrators will have to pay out of the proceeds of any sale of the business in whole or in part.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.

They point to improving sales over October as proof the business had a future.

MPs also laid into the US firm with members of the Business Committee accusing it of "predatory capitalism" and "asset stripping".

Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk

No-one appears to dispute the fact that Gordon Brothers' insistence that they get paid most of their £22.5m debt was a major stumbling block to a sale.

Potential buyers balked at paying out millions on a loan that Gordon Brothers inherited for nothing.

Martin Property Group offered £5m up front with the balance to be deferred, while Xyra Holdings offered £12.5m up front but, according to sources close to the deal, were thought unable to actually pay.

Unsurprisingly perhaps, Gordon Brothers dispute a lot of how they have been characterised.

First, they insist that they lent the business £85m to try to keep it alive for the 17 months since they bought it. Without them, this collapse would have happened in June last year.

The £20m taken out of the business since then has mostly been interest on that loan.

Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with a year earlier, Poundland was not generating enough cash to sustain itself. Sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when Gordon Brothers bought the business - more than offsetting a £100m cost-cutting programme.

Like other retailers Poundland was hit by rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates.

In the end, argue Gordon Brothers, none of the potential buyers could meet their terms and prove they had the money and expertise to make a go of it.

Such is the discrepancy between the two versions that the chair of the Business Committee wants Gordon Brothers and the management back in front of them to get to the truth.

It is still possible that a bidder may emerge in the coming hours and days to save the business as a whole but most industry observers think that looks unlikely.

Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told the BBC: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome. I think realistically, though, there is a chance now that there will be a breakup."

Like previous busts such as Woolworths, BHS and Wilko, many of these stores will find new owners and they will need local, experienced staff.

But none of that will be much comfort to those workers facing grave uncertainty a month before Christmas, when they should be at their busiest and most needed.

Gordon Brothers specialise in situations of commercial distress. When they take on a distressed company, they try to make sure that the worst possible outcome is still one that makes money for them.

In this situation, the worst outcome would mean they get paid back £22.5m, earn interest on the loan they provided the company (secured against the company assets) and a few other miscellaneous fees.

Little wonder then that many people say they had little incentive to strain every sinew to secure a buyer. They argue they kept a business that would have collapsed last June going for another 17 months, which extended employment for thousands of workers.

But if, as some retail veterans have told the BBC, Gordon Brothers never really intended to turn this business around, why would the previous owners PepCo give them a no-lose gamble? Why didn't they do what Gordon Brothers are doing - profiting with no risk?

The answer is simple: Pepco have other businesses, which could have got tangled up in the administration of Poundland.
